Jörg Hegemann recorded a tribute album, A Tribute To Albert Ammons, celebrating his 100th birthday in 2007.

Albert Ayler (; July 13, 1936 – November 25, 1970) was an American avant-garde jazz saxophonist, singer and composer. His trio and quartet records of 1964, such as Spiritual Unity and The Hilversum Session were one of his best known works. Ayler disappeared on November 5, 1970, and he was found dead in New York City's East River on November 25. His death was ruled a suicide. There were rumors that the mafia killed him.

Albert Barillé (14 February 1920 – 5 February 2009) was a Polish-born French television producer, creator, screenwriter, cartoonist, and founder of Procidis. He is the creator of the stop-motion animated series Les Aventures de Colargol, and the series Once Upon a Time.... He was also an author of medical documentaries, theater pieces, and popularized philosophy. Once Upon a Time... The Discoverers (1994)

Albert Camus (7 November 1913 – 4 January 1960) was a French writer and thinker. He wrote novels, plays, essays, and newspaper articles. He also worked in the theatre as a director and an actor. He said that he felt happier among theatre people than among writers. In 1957, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature. He was 43 when the prize was announced and 44 when he received it. Only Rudyard Kipling had received it at a younger age. Camus was born in Algeria, which was then ruled by France. His family was very poor. His father died in World War I when Camus was less than one year old. His mother could not read or write. He grew up in a small flat in a poor working-class area of Algiers. The flat had no running water or electricity. He was able to continue at school because a teacher helped him and because he later received money from the state. His poor childhood and his life in Algeria strongly shaped his later work. Camus is best known for three novels: The Stranger (1942), The Plague (1947), and The Fall (1956). He also wrote two long essays about ideas, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) and The Rebel (1951), as well as four plays of his own. He often wrote about a problem that he called the absurd. Human beings want life to have a clear meaning, but the world gives them no answer. Camus called this conflict the absurd. He said that people should not kill themselves because life has no clear meaning. They should instead see the truth clearly, continue to live, and refuse false hopes. Later, Camus wrote more about revolt. To revolt means to say "no" to something that is wrong or unjust. He believed that revolt could be good, but that it must have limits. He opposed the death penalty and political murder. He refused to support any political system that treated killing as a normal or necessary way to build a better future. However, he was not a pacifist, and he said this clearly. Many people call Camus an existentialist, but he often said that he was not one. He did not want to belong to any complete system of thought. He gave a similar answer when people called him an atheist. Camus also took part in the French resistance against Nazi Germany. He wrote for the secret newspaper Combat and became one of its editors in 1944. After the war, he wrote against the death penalty, the atomic bomb, and totalitarianism. Totalitarianism is a form of government in which the state tries to control every part of public and private life. The war in Algeria caused Camus great pain. He wanted Arab and Berber Algerians to have full political rights, and he publicly called for an end to the colonial system. However, he did not support full independence for Algeria. He hoped instead for a free and federal Algeria that would remain joined to France. In this system, Muslim Algerians and French settlers would have the same rights. He also refused to accept the killing of civilians by either side. In 1956, he went to Algiers and asked both sides to stop attacking civilians. His plan failed. After this, he said very little in public about Algeria, although he continued to help prisoners in private. Camus died in a car crash in 1960, at the age of 46. In the car was the unfinished manuscript of his novel The First Man. The book was published in 1994, thirty-four years after his death. The earliest known member of the Camus family in Algeria was Claude Camus. He was born in Bordeaux in 1809. He and his wife crossed the Mediterranean Sea soon after France began to rule Algeria. Older books often say that the Camus family came from Alsace. Camus also tells this story in The First Man. However, this was probably only a family story. Olivier Todd, one of Camus's biographers, studied the official records and found evidence that the family came from the Bordeaux region instead. This also makes it more likely that they went to Algeria for economic reasons rather than political ones. French troops landed in Algeria in 1830. The fighting continued for many years, while more and more European settlers arrived. By 1848, there were nearly 100,000 settlers in Algeria. They came not only from France, but also from Spain, Italy, and Malta. By 1936, about one million Europeans lived in Algeria. When the Algerian War began in 1954, Europeans made up about one ninth of the population. The children and grandchildren of these settlers later became known as pieds-noirs, which means "black feet" in French. Nobody knows for certain where this name came from. Some people say that it referred to the colour of the settlers' shoes. Others say that it came from the muddy feet of farm workers. Camus belonged to this European settler population. His father's family came from the Bordeaux region, while his mother's family came from Menorca, a Spanish island. The European settlers were French citizens. Most Muslim Algerians were legally French subjects, but they did not have the same rights as citizens or the same political power. Algeria was ruled as three departments of France rather than as a separate country. However, the people who lived there did not have equal rights. This inequality is important for understanding Camus's life and work. Albert Camus was born on 7 November 1913 on a farm near the small town of Mondovi, which is now called Dréan. The town is in eastern Algeria, near Annaba. His father, Lucien Auguste Camus, worked in the wine cellars of a company called Jules Ricôme. He watched over the pressing of the grapes and the sending of the wine. His mother was Catherine Sintès. Her family had come to Algeria from the Spanish island of Menorca. She was one of nine children in a poor family. Albert had one brother, Lucien, who was three years older. World War I began in 1914, and Lucien Camus was called into the French army. He served with the Zouaves, a French army unit formed in North Africa. He was badly wounded at the Battle of the Marne. He died in a military hospital on 11 October 1914, at the age of 28. Albert was less than one year old and never knew his father. His mother kept only a photograph of him and a piece of the shell that had killed him. Lucien Camus is buried at Saint-Brieuc in Brittany. His wife never saw his grave. Albert first visited it in 1947. There was one story about his father that Camus never forgot. His father once got up early to watch a man being killed in public by guillotine. The man had murdered a whole family, and Lucien Camus thought that the punishment was fair. However, the sight made him ill. He came home without speaking, lay down, and was sick for much of the morning. Camus used this story three times: near the end of The Stranger, in The Plague, and in his essay "Reflections on the Guillotine". He also told it again in The First Man. In that book, the story troubles the boy so deeply that he has the same nightmare for the rest of his life. When her husband was called into the army in August 1914, Catherine Camus had no money of her own. She therefore moved with her two sons into her mother's flat in Belcourt, a poor working-class district of Algiers. The family moved there a few weeks before they learned that Lucien Camus had died. The flat was on the top floor and had three small rooms and a kitchen. There were two other flats on the same floor, and the three families shared one toilet in the hall. Until 1930, the flat had no running water and no electricity. An oil lamp hung above the only table, where the family ate and the children did their school work. Six people lived there: Albert, his brother, his mother, his grandmother, and two uncles. Albert and Lucien shared one bed until Albert was seventeen. During the war, his mother worked in a factory where she sorted bullets. Later, she cleaned houses and washed clothes for other people. Catherine Camus could not read or write. She was partly deaf and had difficulty speaking. She said some words wrongly and used very few words. Because of this, she was shy with people she did not know and spoke very little at home. Writers do not agree about the cause of these problems. One family story says that she spoke easily when she was young, but that her speech changed in 1914 when she learned that her husband was dead. Another account says that an illness during childhood left her deaf and made her difficult to understand. She had lived in a village where there was no doctor. Camus loved his mother deeply throughout his life, but they almost never talked. He wrote many times about the silence between them. In The First Man, the main character asks his mother about his dead father but learns almost nothing. The book gives one reason for this silence: poor people have fewer things to remember because their days are much the same and they rarely leave the place where they live. The head of the family was Camus's grandmother, who was also called Catherine. She was a hard, proud, and bitter woman who had also lost her husband when she was young. She took the place of her daughter as the person who raised the two boys. She beat them with a whip made from the dried neck of a bull. Their mother stood nearby and only asked the grandmother not to hit them on the head. Another adult in the flat was Camus's uncle Étienne, who made wooden barrels. He could not speak at all until he was a teenager. After an operation, he learned to speak, but he spoke slowly and used only simple words. He also communicated through sounds and signs. He had a dog and a hunting gun, and he cleaned both of them on the family table. Camus loved him and later placed characters based on him in several of his books. Camus wrote about his childhood many times, but he gave two different pictures of it. In some writings, he showed it as very hard. In others, he remembered it as happy. In 1958, a new edition of his first book was published, and Camus wrote a new preface for it. In this preface, he said that poverty had never been a complete misfortune for him because the light of Algeria had always balanced it. He explained that poverty stopped him from believing that everything in the world was good, while the sun taught him that history was not the only important thing. The family lived in real poverty, but Camus still remembered Belcourt with pleasure. The district had a beach, a library, cinemas, and cafés. French, Spanish, Italian, Maltese, and Jewish people lived there. Camus swam, played in the street, and walked around the town with his friends. The difference between the dark rooms of the family flat and the bright sea remained important in all his writing. He often placed these two images next to each other. Camus began attending the boys' school in Belcourt in 1918. He was a very good pupil and was especially good at reading and writing. His teacher was Louis Germain. Germain saw that the boy was clever, but Camus's grandmother wanted him to leave school and begin earning money. Germain argued with the family and persuaded them to let Albert continue. He then taught Albert and two other boys every day after school so that they could take the examination for a scholarship. Because his father had died in the war, Albert was also a pupille de la nation, or "child of the nation". He and his brother received this official position in May 1920. The French state gave children in this position a small amount of money each year to pay for school materials. Camus won a scholarship and entered the Grand Lycée, the large secondary school in Algiers, in October 1924. Some older books say that he entered it in 1923. His time at the school was interrupted at the end of 1930, when doctors found tuberculosis in his lungs. He later returned, repeated his final year, and completed his secondary studies in 1932. Camus never forgot Louis Germain and always said that the teacher had changed his life. He described Germain as strict but kind. Many years later, after receiving the Nobel Prize, Camus wrote to him and thanked him. Sport was more important to the young Camus than school work. Most of the friends he made before 1930 were friends from sport. He played football, usually as a goalkeeper but sometimes as a forward. He first played for a small club called Association Sportive Montpensier. Around 1928, he joined the junior team of Racing Universitaire Algérois, usually called RUA. This was the sports club of the students of Algiers. Camus was small for his age, but he threw himself at the feet of other players to stop the ball and was often hurt. Many years later, he wrote about football in a magazine for former members of the club. He said that much of what he knew about right and wrong had been learned through sport. A friend once asked him whether he would have chosen football or the theatre if his health had allowed him to choose freely. Camus immediately answered that he would have chosen football. During the winter of 1930, Camus began to cough blood. He was taken to the Mustapha Hospital in Algiers, where doctors found tuberculosis in his right lung. Tuberculosis is a serious disease that often attacks the lungs. Camus had just turned seventeen. At that time, there was no medicine that could cure the disease. Doctors used a treatment called artificial pneumothorax. They pushed air into the space around the lung so that the lung became flat and the sick part could rest. The treatment had to be repeated, often every two weeks. Camus had to return for this treatment many times during his life. In 1942, tuberculosis also attacked his other lung. Some of his friends thought that a football match played in heavy rain had caused the illness. Others said that it began after a ball hit him in the chest while he was playing in goal. Neither football nor being hit by a ball causes tuberculosis. However, hard exercise, poor housing, and too little food can make the disease worse. Tuberculosis changed the whole course of Camus's life. He had to stop playing football in serious competitions. Hard exercise remained dangerous for him, although he continued to swim for many years. The illness later stopped him from becoming a university teacher. It also kept him out of the army during World War II, although he asked to join in 1939. Camus later said something surprising about his illness. He said that it had made him free. Because he knew that he might die young, he felt free to choose the kind of life he wanted to live. After becoming ill, Camus went to live with his aunt Antoinette and her husband, Gustave Acault. Acault was a butcher, and the couple had no children. Life in their home was much easier than life in Belcourt. Camus had a room of his own and ate red meat every day because doctors at the time believed that meat helped people with tuberculosis. Acault was also a serious reader and was known for his free-thinking ideas. He gave his nephew books, including Les Nourritures terrestres by André Gide. Many years later, Camus said that Acault had been a kind of father to him. In October 1930, Camus entered the philosophy class at his school. His new teacher was Jean Grenier, who was 32 years old and had recently arrived in Algeria. Grenier noticed that his best pupil was missing. When he learned that Camus was ill, he took a taxi across Algiers to visit him in the flat in Belcourt. The visit was difficult. Camus said very little, and both the teacher and the pupil felt uncomfortable because of the poverty of the rooms. Ten years later, Camus wrote to Grenier about that visit. He explained that his silence had not meant that he was unfriendly. He also said that Grenier's visit had made him feel that he was not as poor as he had believed. Grenier became the most important teacher in Camus's life. For the next thirty years, he read and judged almost everything that Camus wrote. His comments were often very severe. Camus dedicated two of his early books to him. His illness caused him to lose one year of school. In the spring of 1932, he was still writing essays for Grenier's philosophy class. He entered the khâgne only in October of that year. The khâgne was a special class in Algiers for pupils who hoped to enter the famous higher schools in Paris. Camus then entered the University of Algiers. At first he studied literature, but one year later he changed to philosophy. He had wanted to try to enter the École Normale Supérieure in Paris, one of the most famous schools in France, but he gave up the plan. The second year of preparation that he needed was not offered in Algeria. He also could not pay to live in Paris, and his poor health made the plan even more difficult. Camus always had to work while he was studying. During the summer, he worked in a food shop and in his uncle's butcher shop. He also taught younger pupils, sold car parts, worked as a clerk in a shipping office, and worked in the Algiers city office that gave licences for cars. He hated this last job and later used his experience of office work in The Stranger. After finishing his studies, he also worked at the Institute of Meteorology in Algiers from November 1937 until September 1938. In 1936, Camus completed his final university paper. It was about Christian thought and Neoplatonism, a later school of Greek philosophy. The paper compared Plotinus, a Greek thinker, with Augustine of Hippo, a Christian writer from North Africa. It earned Camus the diplôme d'études supérieures, an advanced university degree. His illness then stopped him from continuing towards a teaching career. A new attack of tuberculosis in 1937 meant that he was not allowed to take the agrégation, the state examination needed to become a university teacher. On 16 June 1934, Camus married Simone Hié. He was twenty years old. Hié was the daughter of a doctor in Algiers and was well known in the small social world of the city. People talked about her clothes and her love affairs. Such behaviour shocked many people in Algiers during the 1930s. She had earlier planned to marry one of Camus's friends, Max-Pol Fouchet. After she married Camus, the two young men never spoke to each other again. In practice, the marriage lasted little more than one year. The couple separated in 1936, but their divorce was not completed until 1940. For a time after the separation, Camus lived with three other students in a house above the bay of Algiers. They called it "the house facing the world". Camus later remembered those months as an unexpected period of happiness in a difficult life. Camus first joined a political group in 1933. It was an anti-fascist movement started by the writers Henri Barbusse and Romain Rolland. Two years later, he joined the French Communist Party. Most writers now say that he joined in 1935, although some older books give the end of 1934. Camus did not join because he believed in Marxism. He later said that he had never read Marx or Engels before joining the party. He told Jean Grenier that he had to become a Communist because he wanted to remain close to the poor people from whom he came. For Camus, joining the party in 1935 meant standing beside writers such as André Gide and André Malraux. It did not mean supporting Stalin or the leaders of the party, who meant little to him. His main work for the party was to bring Arab and Berber people into it. He later said that this work made up about half of everything he did for the party. It was also the first time that he truly met Muslim people who had received the same kind of education as himself. French and Muslim children in colonial Algeria did not normally meet at school or while playing. Camus was never an important party leader and never held a high position. However, he was probably the best-known Communist in the cultural life of Algeria. At first, the Communists in Algeria belonged to the French Communist Party. In 1936, they became a separate Algerian Communist Party. This was the party that later expelled Camus. The Communist Party then changed its political position. Joseph Stalin wanted France to become an ally against Nazi Germany. The Soviet Union therefore told Communist parties in other countries to support the French government. In Algeria, this caused a major change. The Communists had worked with the Algerian nationalist leader Messali Hadj, but they now turned against him, and his movement was banned. Camus refused to accept this change and would not break with the Algerian nationalists. He continued to ask for rights for the Algerian people after the party had ended that campaign. Because of this, he was judged by members of the party and then expelled. Even the local leader Amar Ouzegane, who liked Camus, could not protect him. Writers give slightly different dates for the break. A recent study of all the evidence places it in the autumn of 1937, while an older biography gives November 1937. Camus never joined another political party. He once joked that the only party he could join would be a party of people who were not certain that they were right. In 1936, Camus and a group of young actors created a theatre company called the Théâtre du Travail, which means "Workers' Theatre". Its money came from the Communist House of Culture in Algiers. Their first play was Le Temps du mépris, which was based on a novel by André Malraux. Camus directed the play and also acted in it. Their next work was Révolte dans les Asturies ("Revolt in Asturias"), which Camus and his friends wrote together. It was about a workers' revolt in Spain. The city government of Algiers banned the play before the group could perform it. The House of Culture closed in 1937, and the Théâtre du Travail ended with it. In October 1937, Camus created a new company of his own, the Théâtre de l'Équipe, or "Team Theatre". In the same year, he also directed Prometheus Bound by Aeschylus. This Greek play is about a hero who is punished for helping human beings and refuses to say that he was wrong. Camus loved the theatre throughout his life. He said that he felt happy and relaxed among theatre people, but uncomfortable among writers and thinkers. Camus published his first book in Algiers in 1937. It was called L'Envers et l'endroit. Its English titles include The Wrong Side and the Right Side and Betwixt and Between. The book contains five essays about his childhood, old age, and death. He wrote them in 1935 and 1936 and dedicated the book to Jean Grenier. Only a small number of copies were printed, and the book was not published again until 1958. One of Camus's friends told him that he used the word "I" too often. Camus agreed and said that a writer should remain behind the scenes. His second book was Noces ("Nuptials"), which was printed in Algiers in May 1939. Some books give 1938 instead. It contains four essays about the sun, the sea, and the ruins of Tipasa. Like his first book, it received almost no attention in France. The essay "Nuptials at Tipasa" is the best known of the four. In it, Camus describes a day among Roman ruins beside the sea. He writes that everything there seemed unimportant except the sun, kisses, and the wild smells of the earth. Camus called such moments bonheur, the French word for happiness. For him, this meant short moments in which a person feels completely joined to nature. He believed that such moments should not last too long. At about the same time, Camus began writing his first novel, La Mort heureuse ("A Happy Death"). He did not publish it. It appeared in 1971, many years after his death. In September 1938, Pascal Pia employed Camus as an editorial secretary for a new newspaper called Alger républicain. Pia had been sent from Paris to create the paper. It was published from 6 October 1938 until 28 October 1939. The newspaper said that it spoke for all the people of Algeria, including both Muslims and French settlers. It opposed hatred of Jewish people and the laws that placed Muslim Algerians in a lower position. Camus was not yet twenty-five. Pia employed many young and inexperienced writers because he did not have enough money to pay older journalists. Camus reported on the courts and watched many trials. He later used this experience in The Stranger. He also wrote about a prison ship carrying 609 men. He described its very small cages and lack of light, and wrote that he was ashamed to be there. In July 1939, the police broke up a public meeting held by Algerian nationalists. Camus then wrote a short article called "Unfortunate Arrests" and asked for the arrested men to be freed. Publicly defending Algerian nationalists was unusual and dangerous in colonial Algeria in 1939. Camus published articles under his own name, but he also used several false names. One of them was "Jean Meursault", a name that he later used again for the main character of The Stranger. He also wrote reviews of books. On 20 October 1938, he reviewed La Nausée ("Nausea") by Jean-Paul Sartre. He recognised in the novel an idea close to his own idea of the absurd. However, he thought that the book was too abstract and that Sartre did not make good use of the freedom he gave to his characters. In June 1939, Camus wrote a group of eleven articles about Kabylia, a mountain region of Algeria where many Berber people live. Together, the articles are known as "The Misery of Kabylia". Each article was printed with at least one photograph. Camus travelled to the villages himself. He wrote about poor housing, the lack of clean water, and the small number of doctors. He also gave figures about schools, population, and the age at which people died. He showed that the land was much too crowded. About 247 people lived on each square kilometre, compared with 71 in France. The people ate wheat, whose price had increased, but they grew olives and figs, whose prices had not increased. Many people lived on gifts from others or ate herbs, roots, and thistles because they did not have enough food. In one village, a man showed Camus his young daughter. She was very thin and wore torn clothes. The man asked whether she would not be as beautiful as a French girl if he could give her enough food and better clothes. Camus wrote that he could never forget this meeting. The articles angered the French rulers of Algeria. The governor of Algeria visited Kabylia soon afterwards, although it is difficult to know how much Camus's articles caused the visit. Camus's widow later said that the authorities had tried to pay him to remain silent before the articles were published. Readers have understood the articles in different ways. Many European readers described them as anti-colonial writing, and the Tunisian writer Albert Memmi called them honest and humane. One recent writer believes that this judgement is too generous. He argues that Camus wanted better living conditions for the Kabyle people, but still expected them to remain under French rule. From this point of view, Camus wanted to reform colonialism, not bring it to an end. By 1939, Alger républicain was in serious trouble. Camus and Pia had written against the coming war. When the war began, the government placed censors inside the newspaper office. The censors removed whole articles, and empty spaces appeared on the printed pages because Camus refused to replace the missing words with patriotic writing. He signed some articles with false names and printed passages by older French writers instead. On one occasion, he challenged the censors to remove a passage written by Montaigne. Alger républicain published its final issue on 28 October 1939. Pia and Camus had also started an evening newspaper called Le Soir républicain in September 1939. It continued for a few more months under Camus's direction, but the authorities closed it on 10 January 1940. The owners said that Camus had turned the paper into a personal political campaign. Camus wrote to Jean Grenier that this was true. He said that he had used the newspaper to defend freedom of thought against the censors and to oppose the war without hating anyone. Camus was now without a job and had little hope of finding another one in Algeria because the French colonial authorities did not want him to work there. Foley describes this as a kind of forced exile because the authorities had made it very difficult for Camus to find work in his own country. Pascal Pia found Camus a job in France. Camus arrived in Paris in March 1940 and began working for a large popular newspaper called Paris-Soir. He was an editorial secretary and helped to prepare the pages for printing. He never wrote an article for the paper and did not enjoy the work, but he learned how a large newspaper was produced. The German army attacked France in May 1940. Paris fell in the middle of June, and the newspaper moved south, first to Clermont-Ferrand and then to Lyon. France was divided into two parts. Germany controlled the north and west, while a French government based in Vichy ruled the south. This period is known as Vichy France. On 3 December 1940, Camus married for the second time. His wife was Francine Faure, a mathematics teacher from Oran in Algeria. The wedding was very simple. Pascal Pia and a few people from the newspaper were the only guests. Less than one month later, Camus lost his job because the newspaper had to reduce its staff. Albert and Francine returned to Algeria in January 1941 and lived in Oran. Both of them worked as teachers. Camus did not like the town. He later described it as a town without a soul and as a place that turned its back on the sea. He stayed there for about a year and a half. He could not find regular work, and his health became worse. He taught at a private school for Jewish pupils run by his friend André Bénichou. The children had been removed from state schools because of the laws of the Vichy government. In February 1941, while living in Oran, Camus completed The Myth of Sisyphus. In May 1942, the Paris publisher Gallimard published L'Étranger. The book is known in English as either The Stranger or The Outsider. Later in the same year, Gallimard published Le Mythe de Sisyphe ("The Myth of Sisyphus"). Both books were published in Paris while the city was under German rule. The Stranger appeared in May, when Camus was still living in Algeria. By the time The Myth of Sisyphus was published, he was ill and staying at Le Panelier in the mountains of France. The two books made Camus famous very quickly, and they remain his best-known works. Much of the early success of The Stranger came from a long essay by Jean-Paul Sartre called "Explication de L'Étranger". It was published in the magazine Cahiers du Sud in February 1943. Sartre praised the novel and its plain style, but he was not sure that Camus had fully understood the German and Danish thinkers whose ideas he used. The Stranger is told by a man named Meursault, who works as a clerk in Algiers. The book begins with the death of his mother. Meursault travels to the home for old people where she has lived for several years. He sits beside her body during the night, as people expect him to do. However, he smokes a cigarette, drinks coffee, and falls asleep for a short time. He does not ask to see her face for the last time. He does not know her exact age, and he does not cry. The next day, he goes swimming and meets Marie Cardona, a young woman from his office. He takes her to see a comic film and spends the night with her. After this, his life continues as before. Marie asks whether he loves her. He answers that the word does not mean anything to him, but says that he will marry her if she wants. A neighbour named Raymond Sintès, who is said to make money from women, asks Meursault to write a letter to his Arab mistress. Later, Raymond also asks him to speak for him at the police station. Meursault agrees because agreeing costs him nothing. Meursault, Marie, and Raymond visit a friend's hut beside the sea. A group of Arab men follows them. There is a short fight, and Raymond is cut with a knife. Later, Meursault walks alone in the strong midday sun and meets one of the men again. He shoots him once and then fires four more bullets into his body. During the trial, the court says very little about the killing itself. Instead, it speaks mainly about the funeral. Witnesses say that Meursault did not want to see his mother's body, that he smoked, slept, and drank coffee beside it, that he did not cry, and that he did not know her age. The prosecutor calls Meursault a monster with an empty heart and asks for him to be put to death. He says almost nothing about the man who was killed on the beach. Meursault's own lawyer uses the same kind of argument and asks him to say things that are not true. Meursault refuses. He is sentenced to death. The same ideas return throughout the book: everything is the same to him, nothing is his fault, and nothing matters. At the end, while waiting in his prison cell, he refuses to speak with a priest. He then finds a kind of peace in the thought that the world is as uncaring about him as he is about it. The Arab man whom Meursault kills is never given a name. Later writers have paid much attention to this fact. Readers also warn against a common mistake: Meursault should not simply be understood as Camus speaking for himself. Scholars still disagree about how close the character is to his author. The novel has been understood in many different ways. Some read it as a story about the absurd. Others see Meursault as a man who refuses the lies of society. Some understand the novel mainly through the colonial world of Algeria, while others see it as a trap that tests the reader's own judgement. Camus said that he had three real people in mind when he created Meursault and that he himself was one of the three. In August 1942, Camus went to a small place called Le Panelier in the mountains of the Haute-Loire. His doctor had advised him to breathe mountain air. Le Panelier is near the village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon. During the war, many people in Le Chambon and the villages around it worked together to hide Jewish refugees. Yad Vashem in Israel gave the title Righteous Among the Nations to about forty people from the village. It also honoured the rescue work of the community as a whole. Francine returned to Algeria, and Camus planned to join her in November. However, the war changed everything. American forces landed in North Africa in November 1942. The German army then occupied the south of France, and all travel and communication between France and Algeria were cut. Camus could not leave France. He and Francine remained apart until she arrived in Paris in the autumn of 1944, almost two years later. This forced separation later became part of The Plague, in which a whole town is closed and families are separated from one another. In 1943, Pascal Pia was working for the secret resistance newspaper Combat. He asked Camus to join him. Camus moved to Paris near the end of the year. He prepared pages, corrected and edited articles, and wrote articles of his own. For safety, he did not sign them. The articles he wrote in 1944 attacked the German army and secret police. They also attacked Marshal Pétain and the Vichy government. They warned French people who helped the Germans that they would be judged after the war. The work was dangerous. Several members of Combat were arrested, sent to prison camps, or killed. One of them was the poet René Leynaud, a friend of Camus who was shot by the Germans in 1944. Writers give different dates for the time when Camus became the head of the newspaper. Some say that Pia made him editor of the secret paper in 1943. Others say that Pia left in June 1944 to do other resistance work and that Camus took his place at that time. In 1943, Camus also began working for the publisher Gallimard. He remained there until his death. He read new books for the company and directed a series of books of his own. Camus wrote four short essays called "Letters to a German Friend". They are not true letters. They are written as speeches to a German who never answers, and the German is not a real person. Camus wrote the first essay in July 1943, and it appeared in the secret magazine Revue Libre. The second was signed with the false name Louis Neuville and published in Cahiers de la Libération. The third appeared in 1945 in Libertés. The fourth was not published separately. It appeared when all four essays were published together as a book in 1945. Camus dedicated the book to René Leynaud. In these essays, Camus explains why France was slow to fight against Germany. He says that the French needed moral reasons for fighting and could not depend only on love of country. In the final essay, he makes an important argument. He and his German friend began with the same belief: that the world has no meaning. However, they followed different paths. The German chose war and conquest. Camus chose justice. He wrote that although the world itself has no meaning, one thing within it does have meaning: the human being. Human beings matter because they are the only beings who ask for meaning. This is the point at which Camus's idea of the absurd begins to become an idea about how human beings should treat one another. Paris was freed in August 1944. Combat could now be published openly. Camus wrote its leading articles, with titles such as "The Blood of Freedom" and "The Night of Truth". On 21 August, the newspaper welcomed the freeing of the city with an article by Camus called "From Resistance to Revolution". About 200,000 copies were printed. For a time, Combat was seen as the voice of the French Resistance. Many of its readers were young teachers, students, and members of trade unions. Camus became a well-known public figure almost at once. He also used the newspaper to explain what he thought journalism should be. He wrote that newspapers should be free from the control of money. He said that it was better to report true news second than to report false news first. A newspaper should help its readers to understand events clearly instead of only trying to please them. Camus asked Jean-Paul Sartre to write for Combat. Sartre reported on the street fighting during the liberation of Paris. In 1945, Camus sent him to the United States as the newspaper's correspondent. Camus remained at Combat until 1947. He left after arguments inside the newspaper and financial problems that would have forced it to give up its independence. After the war, France had to judge the people who had helped the German forces. This period is called the épuration, or purge. At first, Camus supported severe punishment. He wrote that a country that failed to remove guilty people from public life would also fail to rebuild itself. The Catholic writer François Mauriac disagreed with him and asked for mercy. In January 1945, the writer Robert Brasillach, who had supported Germany, was sentenced to death. Camus was asked to sign a request to Charles de Gaulle to save Brasillach's life. Camus signed the request and explained his reason in a letter. He said that he had always been deeply against the death penalty and that the least he could do was refuse to take part in it. He also said that he had no respect for Brasillach, either as a writer or as a man. The request failed, and Brasillach was shot. Camus soon understood that the purge was not fair. Some people were punished severely, while many others who were also guilty were never judged. In 1948, Camus said publicly that Mauriac had been right. His articles from the war are still difficult to judge because he asked for quick and strong justice even though he opposed the death penalty throughout his life. He later said that the purge had taught him an important lesson: justice that tries to become complete and perfectly pure stops being justice. On 6 August 1945, an American aircraft dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima in Japan. About 80,000 people died at once. Most French newspapers welcomed the event and described it as a great victory. Camus wrote against the bombing on 8 August.

Albert Fert (born 7 March 1938) is a French physicist. He discovered giant magnetoresistance which was used to make gigabyte hard disks much easier to build. He is a professor at Université Paris-Sud in Orsay and scientific director of a laboratory called Unité mixte de recherche. The laboratory is part of the Centre national de la recherche scientifique (National Scientific Research Centre) and Thales Group. He was awarded the 2007 Nobel Prize in Physics together with the German physicist Peter Grünberg. Fert graduated in 1962 from the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. He received his master's degree in 1963 at the University of Paris, and earned his PhD in 1970 at the Université Paris-Sud. In 1988 Fert discovered Giant magnetoresistance (GMR) in iron and chromium which began spintronics; GMR was also discovered by Peter Grünberg from the Jülich Research Centre but Peter Grünberg did not work with Fert. Since 1988, Albert Fert has helped to improve spintronics. In 2004 he was elected to the French Academy of Sciences. In 2009 he was elected to the Academia Europaea. American Physical Society International Prize for New Materials (1994) Grand prix de physique Jean Ricard of the French Physical Society (1994) International Union of Pure and Applied Physics Magnetism Award (1994) Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique Gold Medal (2003)

Albert Coates (born Saint Petersburg, 23 April 1882; died Cape Town, 11 December 1953) was an Anglo-Russian conductor and composer. Coates was born in Saint Petersburg, Russia, the youngest of seven sons of an English father and a Russian mother. He studied at the conservatory in Leipzig, where his greatest teacher was Arthur Nikisch. He worked at the opera house in Dresden, and became conductor at Saint Petersburg's Mariinsky Theatre. After the Russian Revolution and World War I he just managed to escape from Russia in April 1919. He first appeared at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden in 1914 conducting Richard Wagner's Tristan und Isolde. He was a man with a lot of energy, and he introduced the audiences to a lot of music they had not heard, especially by Russian composers such as Alexander Scriabin, but also English music by Ralph Vaughan Williams, Arnold Bax, and Gustav Holst, whose suite The Planets he gave the first complete London public performance. In the 1920s and early 1930s he often worked with the London Symphony Orchestra. He made gramophone recordings in the very early days of the gramophone. These include Scriabin's Poème de l'Extase and many bits from Wagner's Der Ring des Nibelungen and (in 1925) the complete Symphony No. 9 of Beethoven. He was the conductor for the first recording of Rachmaninoff's Piano Concerto No. 3, with Vladimir Horowitz as soloist. In 1925 he gave the first stage performance outside Russia of Rimsky-Korsakov's opera The Legend of the Invisible City of Kitezh and the Maiden Fevroniya. He composed several works including operas and a symphonic poem The Eagle, dedicated to the memory of his former teacher Artur Nikisch, which was performed in Leeds in 1925. In 1946 he settled in Milnerton, Cape Town, South Africa, where he died in 1953. Albert Coates was no relation to Eric Coates, the English composer of light music, nor to the tenor John Coates.

Albert Claude (24 August 1899 – 22 May 1983) was a Belgian biologist. He shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1974 with Christian de Duve and George Emil Palade. He went to the University of Liège. In the summer of 1929 he joined the Rockefeller Institute. He worked at Rockefeller University in the 1930s and 1940s. In 1949, he became Director of the Institut Jules Bordet in Brussels. He worked there until 1970.

Albert Finney (9 May 1936 – 7 February 2019) was a British actor. His career lasted 60 years. Finney was mostly known for his role in Tom Jones, for his role as Hercule Poirot in Murder on the Orient Express and for his role as Edward Bloom in Big Fish. He won a Golden Globe Award, a Screen Actors Guild Award, an Emmy Award, and a BAFTA Award. He was also the voice of Finis Everglot in Tim Burton's Corpse Bride. Finney was born in Salford, Greater Manchester on 9 May 1936. He was educated at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Arts. Finney married Jane Wenham from 1957 to 1961. Finney married Anouk Aimée from 1970 to 1978. He married Pene Delmage in 2006. He had a son, Simon. In May 2011, Finney received treatment for kidney cancer. Finney died from a respiratory tract infection on 7 February 2019. Finney declined the offer of a CBE in 1980, as well as a knighthood in 2000. He criticised these honours as "perpetuating snobbery".

Albert Lawrence Brooks (born Albert Lawrence Einstein; July 22, 1947) is an American actor, comedian, director, and screenwriter. He is known for his roles in Modern Romance (1981), Lost in America (1985), Defending Your Life (1991), Finding Nemo (2003), The Simpsons Movie (2007), and Drive (2011). Brooks was born in Beverly Hills, California.

Albert Dekker (December 20, 1905 – May 5, 1968) was an American character actor and politician. He was best known for his roles in Dr. Cyclops, The Killers, Kiss Me Deadly, and The Wild Bunch. He was born in Brooklyn, New York. He served as a member of the California State Assembly from 1945 through 1947 as a Democrat. Dekker was found dead at his home in Hollywood, California by his fiancée Jeraldine Saunders on May 5, 1968. He was 62 years old. He was naked, kneeling in the bathtub, with a noose tightly wrapped around his neck and looped around the shower curtain rod. His death was ruled to be an accidental case of erotic asphyxiation. Dekker has a star, in the motion picture category, on the Hollywood Walk of Fame at 6620 Hollywood Boulevard.

Albert Boadella Oncins (born 30 July 1943) is a Spanish actor and playwright. He was the director of the company of the independent theater Els Joglars until 2012. Boadella was born in Barcelona. In 2003 he wrote the screenplay and directed the movie Buen viaje, excelencia, a caricature of the last months of life of the general Franco. In December 2012 he was awarded the Alfonso Ussía awards in the category of Person of the Year, together with Arturo Fernández.

Albert Mkrtchyan (, February 27, 1937 – February 28, 2018); Armenian movie director, screenwriter, and actor. He was honored with the People's Artist of the Republic of Armenia (2003). He was born in Gyumri, Soviet Union. His best known works are The Tango of Our Childhood, Tghamardik and The Song of the Old Days. Mkrtchyan died on February 28, 2018 in Yerevan, Armenia, one day after his 81st birthday.

Rodolphe Albert Millaire, CC, CQ (January 18, 1935 – August 15, 2018) was a Canadian actor and theatre director. He was known for his roles on stage in Tartuffe, Le Misanthrope, Dom Juan. He also appeared in Canadian sitcoms such as Heart of Rose and Cyrano de Bergerac. Millaire died of prostate cancer in Montreal on August 15, 2018, aged 83.

Albert "Tootie" Heath (May 31, 1935 – April 3, 2024) was an American jazz hard bop drummer. He is the brother of saxophonist Jimmy Heath and the bassist Percy Heath. In 1975, the brothers formed the Heath Brothers. He notably worked with musicians such as John Coltrane, J. J. Johnson, Wes Montgomery, Art Farmer and Benny Golson's Jazztet, Cedar Walton, Bobby Timmons, Kenny Drew, Sonny Rollins, Dexter Gordon, Johnny Griffin, Herbie Hancock, Friedrich Gulda, Nina Simone and Yusef Lateef. Heath was born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Heath died from leukemia in Santa Fe, New Mexico, on April 3, 2024, at the age of 88.

Ludwig Philipp Albert Schweitzer, MD, OM, (14 January 1875 – 4 September 1965) was a French-German theologian, musician, philosopher and physician. He was born in Kaysersberg (Alsace), at the time a part of the German Empire. He wrote books about music and religion. He started a famous hospital in Lambarene, Africa. He received the 1952 Nobel Peace Prize. Albert Schweitzer was born in Kaysersberg (Alsace), on 14 January 1875. He lived in the village of Gunsbach, where his father was a local pastor. His father taught him how to play music. In 1893, Schweitzer passed his Baccalaureat. After this, Schweitzer went to Paris to learn philosophy and music, before returning to his birthplace to study theology. He spent nine years studying medicine and surgery. He would dedicate his life to helping people and curing diseases. Schweitzer was a famous organist and was extremely interested in the music of Johann Sebastian Bach. He developed a simple style of performance, which he thought to be closer to what Bach had meant. In 1908, he completed the final version of his book "Johann Sebastian Bach". In the book, he argued for the new style, which has had great influence on the way Bach’s music is now treated. When Schweitzer was in Lambarene, his main recreation was to play Bach’s music. He also gave musical performances to raise money for medical supplies in Gabon. Recordings of Schweitzer playing the music of Bach are available on CD. Between 1934 and 1935, he had a trial recording for HMV on the organ of the old Queen's Hall in London. In mid-December 1935, he began to record for Columbia Records on the organ of All-Hallows-by-the-Tower, Barking, London. Schweitzer became well known for his books on Jesus and Christianity. He was not so much interested in the historical study of Jesus, as in the Christian idea of the end of the world, which can be found in the Bible and the teachings of Jesus. Schweitzer also served as a minister for Saint Nicholas Church in Strassburg. In the philosophy of Albert Schweitzer, the most important idea is the respect for life. In his book "The Philosophy of Civilization", he wrote that "true philosophy" begins with the idea that: Albert Schweitzer’s ethical principles meant that he tried to have a personal and spiritual relationship with the universe. It also meant that he was vegetarian. Albert Schweitzer spent most of his life in Lambaréné, Africa. In 1904, he was inspired to help sick people in the world, so he studied medicine. After his medical studies in 1913, he went to Lambaréné with his wife to establish a hospital that would serve thousands of Africans. During World War I, the French made Schweitzer and his wife, both Germans, leave Africa. In 1924, he returned to Lambaréné and managed to rebuild the destroyed hospital, where he served as a physician. From 1939-1948, he stayed in Lambarene since he could not go to Europe during the war. Three years later he resumed his medical practices. But he was no longer just a medical doctor and whenever possible he went to Europe to lecture at universities. Slowly his ideas become known, not only in Europe but worldwide. In 1952 Dr Albert Schweitzer was awarded The Nobel Prize for peace. He gave a famous speech "The Problem of Peace". He died on 4 September 1965 at his hospital in Lambarene.

Albert Charles Paul Marie Roussel (5 April 1869 - 23 August 1937) was a French composer. Roussel spent seven years as a midshipman. He only turned to music as an adult. But he then became one of the most important composers of the years between the two world wars. His earlier music came from the impressionism of Debussy and Ravel. He turned more towards neoclassicism with his later music. Albert Roussel was born in Tourcoing (Nord department of France). HIs earliest interest was not music. It was mathematics. He spent some time in the French Navy. In 1889 and 1890 he served on the crew of the frigate Iphigénie. These travels were significant to his later career as a composer. This is because many of his musical works would reflect his interest in far-off and interesting places. After Roussel left the Navy in 1894, he began to study music with Eugène Gigout. He continued his studies until 1908 at the Schola Cantorum (one of his teachers there was Vincent d'Indy). While he studied, he would also teach at the Schola. His fellow students were Erik Satie and the young Edgard Varèse. During World War I, he served as an ambulance driver on the Western Front. After the war, he bought a summer house in Normandy. This is where he gave most of his time to composing music. Roussel was a classicist. Some of his first works are very much like impressionism. But he soon found a style fit just for him. This style had a strong rhythmic sound. The Schola Cantorum left a mark on Roussel's mature writing. Compared with the style of other French composers like Gabriel Fauré or Claude Debussy, Roussel's orchestration is rather powerful and heavy. Roussel also liked jazz. He wrote a piano-vocal composition called Jazz dans la nuit. This has a lot in common with other jazz-influenced works such as the "Blues" second movement of Maurice Ravel's Violin Sonata. Roussel's most important pieces include his ballets. They are Le festin de l'araignée, Bacchus et Ariane, and Aeneas. Among his other works are four symphonies (the Third is the most often played), a piano concerto, a concertino for cello and orchestra, a psalm setting for chorus and orchestra, music for the theater, solo piano music, and songs. He died in the town of Royan in western France in 1937. That is the same year that his countrymen Ravel, Charles-Marie Widor, and Gabriel Pierné died. Arturo Toscanini included the suite from the ballet Le festin de l'araignée in one of his concerts with the NBC Symphony Orchestra. Georges Prêtre recorded this same music with the Orchestre National de France for EMI in 1984. Pavie). f.p. Albert Paulsen (Albert Paulson; December 13, 1925 – April 25, 2004) was an Ecuadorian-American actor. His career began during the 1960s. He appeared in many television comedy shows. He worked with Bob Hope, Johnny Carson, and George Burns. He won a Emmy Award in 1964. Paulsen died from natural causes, aged 78.

Albertus Petrus Enricus Gerardus Westelaken (2 September 1949 – 4 June 2015), better known by his stage name Albert West, was a Dutch pop singer and record producer. He was the lead singer of The Shuffles from 1963 to 1973. He was born in 's-Hertogenbosch, North Brabant.

Albert Rohan (9 May 1936 – 4 June 2019) was an Austrian diplomat. He was Permanent Secretary of the Austrian Foreign Ministry from 1996 to 2001. Rohan was born in Melk, Lower Austria. From 1977 to 1981, he was Director at the Executive Office of the United Nations Secretary General. Rohan died in Vienna on 5 June 2019 at the age of 83.

Alberta Hunter (April 1, 1895 – October 17, 1984) was an American singer-songwriter. She sang blues and jazz music. She was especially popular in the 1920s and 1930s. She sang the critically acclaimed "Downhearted Blues" in 1922. She stopped performing in the 1950s. Hunter was born in Memphis, but later moved to Chicago. Hunter was a lesbian. Hunter died in New York City at age 89.

Alberta Adams (born Roberta Louise Osborn on July 26, 1917 - December 25, 2014) was an American Detroit blues, jump blues, and Chicago blues singer. Adams was born in Indianapolis, Indiana. She was raised in Detroit, she began performing as a tap dancer and nightclub singer in the 1930s. In 1952, she landed a recording contract with Chess Records and recorded alongside Red Saunders for the record label. Adams toured alongside Duke Ellington, Eddie Vinson, Louis Jordan, Lionel Hampton, and T-Bone Walker amongst others. Her solo career saw her secure a recording contract with the now defunct Cannonball Records, and she recorded two albums for them: 1999's Born With the Blues and 2000s Say Baby Say. Her 2004 album, I'm on the Move, was released on Eastlawn Records label. In 2006 she released the EP Detroit's Queen of the Blues, which was named Outstanding Blues/R&B Recording at the 2006 Detroit Music Awards. At age 91 she recorded Detroit Is My Home, with Ann Rabson and Thornetta Davis as guest artists. Adams died in Detroit, Michigan after a period of failing health, aged 97.

Alberto Cortez (born José Alberto García Gallo; 11 March 1940 – 4 April 2019) was an Argentine singer and songwriter. During his career, he released more than forty albums. In 1960, he famously covered the song "Sucu Sucu". He was born in Rancul, La Pampa Province. Cortez died of a gastrointestinal hemorrhage on 4 April 2019 in Madrid, the capital city of Spain. He was 79.

Alberto Carpani (April 23, 1956 – May 11, 2020) was an Italian singer. He was best known for his Italo disco releases in the late 1970's and early 1980's as Albert One, and his Eurodance release "Sing a Song Now Now" in 1999 as A.C. One. He was also a DJ and music producer. He was born in Pavia, Italy. Carpani died of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on May 11, 2020 in Portofino, Italy at the age of 64.

Alberto Sordi (15 June 1920 – 24 February 2003) was an Italian actor, singer, composer, comedian, director and screenwriter.Sordi won seven David di Donatello awards. It is Italy's most honorable movie award. He also received a Golden Lion for lifetime achievement at the Venice Film Festival in 1995. He also won a Golden Globe Award.

Alberto Testa (23 December 1922 – 4 October 2019) was an Italian dancer, choreographer, dance critic and teacher. He was born in Turin. He choreographed many ballets of operatic music, and worked on movies mainly with Franco Zeffirelli and Luchino Visconti. Testa died in Turin on October 4, 2019 of pneumonia at the age of 96.

Alberto Naranjo [nah-rahn'-ho] (September 14, 1941 – January 27, 2020) was a Venezuelan jazz musician and composer. In 1992, he was nominated for a Grammy Award. Naranjo made arrangements for the groups Conexion Latina, Guaco and Mango; pop-artists like Ilan Chester, Simón Díaz, Oscar D'León, Ricardo Montaner, María Rivas, Aldemaro Romero and Adalberto Santiago

Alberto Moioli, (Monza, February 19, 1968), is an Italian art critic and writer, editorial director of the Enciclopedia d'arte italiana from 2012 to 2021. Enciclopedia d’Arte Italiana, General catalog of artists from 900 to today, n.1, Milan, 2012. Enciclopedia d’Arte Italiana, General catalog of artists from 900 to today, n.2, Milan, 2013. Alci Acosta (born Alcibiades Alfonso Acosta Cervantes on 5 November 1938) is a Colombian bolero singer, pianist, and performer of Latin American music including pasillos, corridos, valses, and rancheras. Acosta is a highly successful artist throughout Latin America having partnered with other notable artists such as Ecuadorian singer, Julio Jaramillo, who died in 1978. Acosta's best-selling single to date is "Traicionera" which has sold over 1,300,000 copies across Latin America. Other notable hits are "La Cárcel De Sing Sing", "La Copa Rota", "Hola Soledad", "Tango Negro", "Señora Bonita", "El Preso Número 9", and "El Contragolpe". Acosta has released numerous albums over his career including Tropicales Ilegales, 16 Éxitos De Oro, Mis Mejores Canciones, and Solo Hits (a compilation of hit singles). Acosta is the father of singer, Checo Acosta (born on 14 June 1965).

Aldemaro Romero (March 12, 1928 – September 15, 2007) was a Venezuelan pianist, composer, arranger and orchestral conductor. He was born in Valencia, Carabobo State. Romero was a prolific composer, creating a wide range of music, such as Caribbean, Jazz, Venezuelan waltzes, including works for orchestra, orchestra and soloist, orchestra and choir, chamber music, up to symphonic works of great dimensions. In 1951 Romero signed contract with RCA Victor to record with a full orchestra, what was to be a very successful album in the "Dinner In..." series, featuring popular Latin American music. Under the RCA label he published his LP Dinner in Caracas, with which beat all sales records in South America until then. Afterwards, recorded numerous LP albums in different countries. In America, his ability as arranger/conductor led him to collaborate with popular orchestras and singers, such as Dean Martin, Jerry Lee Lewis, Stan Kenton, Machito and Tito Puente, among others. He also toured extensively, performing in numerous countries: Mexico, Puerto Rico, Colombia, Peru, Brazil, Argentina, Spain, France, Greece, Switzerland, Sweden, Italy, Russia, Egypt and Japan. Romero was the creator of a new form of Venezuelan music, known as "New Wave" (Onda Nueva), derived from the joropo and influenced by Brazilian Bossa Nova. He also had an important role in the field of learned music. Aldemaro Romero died in Caracas on September 15, 2007, at the age of 79.

Alden Caleb Ehrenreich (; born November 22, 1989) is an American actor. He won a Tony Award in 2026. In 2013, he appeared in Woody Allen's Blue Jasmine and Park Chan-wook's Stoker. In 2016, Ehrenreich starred as Hobie Doyle in the Coen brothers comedy Hail, Caesar! and for his leading role in Warren Beatty's romantic comedy-drama Rules Don't Apply. He played Han Solo in 2018's Solo: A Star Wars Story.

Aldo Ciccolini (, 15 August 1925 – 1 February 2015), was an Italian-French pianist. He was born in Naples, Italy. He taught at the Conservatoire de Paris from 1970 to 1988. His students included Akiko Ebi, Géry Moutier, Jean-Yves Thibaudet, Artur Pizarro, Nicholas Angelich, André Sayasov and Jean-Luc Kandyoti. Ciccolini died at the age of 89 on 1 February 2015 at his home in Paris.

Aldir Blanc Mendes (2 September 1946 – 4 May 2020) was a Brazilian songwriter. He co-composed many songs with singer-songwriter João Bosco, guitarist Guinga, and others. He was born in Rio de Janeiro. Elis Regina recorded several of his songs such as "O bêbado e a equilibrista". Blanc's work from 1972 to 1987, he was analyzed by Charles A. Perrone in Masters of Contemporary Brazilian Song MPB 1965–1985. Blanc died of COVID-19 on 4 May 2020 in Rio de Janeiro at the age of 73.

Aldis Alexander Basil Hodge (born September 20, 1986) is an American actor. He is known for playing Alec Hardison on Leverage, MC Ren in the 2015 biopic Straight Outta Compton, Levi Jackson in the 2016 movie Hidden Figures, and as Noah on Underground.

Sir Alec Guinness (2 April 1914 - 5 August 2000) was an Academy Award winning English actor. He was born in London. He is well known for the role of Obi-Wan Kenobi, a "Jedi master", in the Star Wars movie series (Episodes IV, V, and VI), a role that he was embarrassed with. He won an Academy Award for "Best Actor in a Leading Role". He got this award for acting in the movie The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957). Guinness also received a Golden Globe Award and a BAFTA Award for that movie. He has also received a Tony Award. In 1989 he received a BAFTA Academy Fellowship Award, a lifetime achievement award. Guinness died from liver cancer in Midhurst, West Sussex, in 2000.

Alexander Rae "Alec" Baldwin III (born April 3, 1958) is an American actor, comedian, and movie producer. He is the oldest and the most well-known of the Baldwin brothers, a family in movies and television. His career has brought him Academy Award, Emmy, and Golden Globe nominations. He has hosted Saturday Night Live several times, including as Donald Trump. He played the television executive Jack Donaghy in the NBC sitcom 30 Rock. Alec Baldwin was born in Amityville, New York and raised in Massapequa, New York. He has three younger brothers, actors Daniel (born 1960), William (born 1963) and Stephen (born 1965). He also has two sisters. They were all raised Roman Catholic. On October 21, 2021, Baldwin was filming on the set of Western movie Rust at the Bonanza Creek Ranch in Santa Fe, New Mexico, when he fired a gun used as a prop, accidentally killing cinematographer Halyna Hutchins and wounding movie director Joel Souza. As to the scene, he was expected to fire the gun, which should have contained blanks. According to court records, Baldwin had been told the gun was safe to use. On January 19, 2023, Santa Fe's district attorney said that Baldwin would be charged with involuntary manslaughter; The charges would filed at the end of January. In April 2023, the charges against Baldwin were dropped. On July 13, 2024, A judge dismisses the manslaughter trial against Alec Baldwin due to withholding of evidence, the trial had started on July 9.

Alec Newman (born 27 November 1974) is a Scottish actor. He is best known for portraying Paul Atreides in the Sci Fi Channel's 2000 mini-series adaptation of Frank Herbert's Dune. He works in film, TV, theatre and video games. In 2025, he won a BAFTA award for his performance in the video game Still Wakes the Deep. In February 2013, Newman became engaged to Heather Stewart. They married in Ayrshire in June 2014.

Aled Jones, (born 29 December 1970) is a Welsh singer and radio and television presenter. He is known for working with BBC and ITV, and radio (for BBC Radio Wales and Classic FM). He presented Daybreak (2012–2014). For the BBC, he has presented Cash in the Attic (2010–2012), Escape to the Country (2010–2013) and Going Back Giving Back (2016–present).

María Alejandra Ana Da Passano (26 July 1947 – 30 June 2014), better known as Alejandra Da Passano, was an Argentine actress of movies, stage plays and television shows. Her best known roles were in Mr. President (1970), Malevo (1972) and La madre María (1974). She was born in Buenos Aires. Da Passano died on 30 June 2014 in Buenos Aires, aged 66.

Alejandro Enrique Planchart (July 29, 1935 – April 28, 2019) was a Venezuelan-American musicologist, conductor and composer. He was thought to be one of the leading experts on the music of Guillaume Du Fay. He was also an expert on music of the Middle Ages and early Renaissance. He taught at Yale University and the University of California, Santa Barbara. He was born in Caracas. Planchart died on April 28, 2019 in Santa Barbara, California. He was 83.

Gabriela Alejandra Guzmán Pinal (born February 9, 1968), known professionally as Alejandra Guzmán, and nicknamed "La Reina de Corazones" (The Queen of Hearts) is a Mexican musician, singer, composer, and actress. She won a Latin Grammy. She is one of the most successful Mexican female singers. She is the daughter of actress Silvia Pinal and singer Enrique Guzmán.
Alejandra Espinoza Cruz (March 27, 1987) is a Mexican Beauty Queen, Actress and TV Host, in 2007 she would win the Univision's beauty pageant/reality show Nuestra Belleza Latina.

Alejandro Sieveking Campano (5 September 1934 – 5 March 2020) was a Chilean playwright, theatre director and actor. He was one of the founders of the Teatro del Ángel (Angel Theatre Company) in Chile and Costa Rica. In 2017, he was awarded the National Prize for Performing and Audiovisual Arts. His theatre credits include Mi hermano Cristián (1957), Ánimas de día claro (1962), La remolienda (1965), Tres tristes tigres (1967) and Ingenuas palomas (1989). Sieveking was born in Rengo, O'Higgins. He married actress Bélgica Castro in 1961. On 5 March 2020, Sieveking died in Santiago at the age of 85. His wife died the next day.

Alek Wek (born 16 April 1977) is a South Sudanese-British model and designer. She began her fashion career at the age of 18 in 1995. She has been praised for her influence on the perception of beauty in the fashion industry. Wek was born in Wau, Sudan (now South Sudan). She is from the Dinka ethnic group. She fled to Britain in 1991 to escape the civil war in Sudan. As of 2009, she lives in Brooklyn, New York, United States. In 2015, she was listed as one of BBC's 100 Women.

Alejandro Sánchez Pizarro (Born, December 18, 1968), known artistically as Alejandro Sanz, is a Spanish singer-songwriter and composer. Sanz was married to Mexican model and actress Jaydy Michel. Their marriage took place in Bali on December 30, 1999, but was not legally recognized in either of the couple's countries of origin. They have a daughter together, Manuela Sánchez Michel, born in Madrid in 2001. Sanz and Michel divorced in 2005.

Aleksandra Nikolayevna Pakhmutova (; born November 9, 1929) is a Russian composer. She has remained one of the best known figures in Soviet and later Russian popular music since she first achieved fame in her homeland in the 1960s.

Aleksandr Yakovlevich Mikhailov (; born 4 October 1944) is a Soviet and Russian actor. He has appeared in 42 movies since 1973. He starred in the 1981 movie Muzhiki! which was in the 32nd Berlin International Film Festival. He became a People's Artist of the RSFSR (1992). and People's Artist of the Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic (2014). Mikhailov was born in Olovyannaya, Russia. He studied at the Maly Theater.

Alexander Anatolyevich Shirvindt (, 19 July 1934 – 15 March 2024) was a Soviet-Russian actor and screenwriter. He was honored with the People's Artist and Meritorious Artist of the RSFSR. He was born in Moscow. He appeared in Grandads-Robbers (1971), The Irony of Fate (1975), The Twelve Chairs (1976), Three Men in a Boat (1979), Station for Two (1982) and The Irony of Fate 2 (2007). He voiced Aramis in Dog in Boots movie. Shirvindt died on 15 March 2024 at a hospital in Moscow, Russia from heart failure at the age of 89.

Aleksandra Kornhauser Frazer (26 September 1926 - 17 May 2020) was a Slovenian chemist and environmentalist. She was a Professor of Chemistry at the Faculty of Natural Sciences and Engineering and Director at the International Centre for Chemical Studies, of the University of Ljubljana, Slovenia. In 1988, she was elected as a member of Academia Europaea. She was professionally active until the age of 90, when she ended her term as the dean of Jožef Stefan International Postgraduate School. She received the Zois Prize for life-time achievements in 1997, the highest prize in the scientific field in Slovenia. She was also an honorary citizen of Ljubljana. She died in Ljubljana on 17 May 2020 at the age of 93.

Aleksandra Evgenievna Yakovleva (born Aleksandra Evgenievna Ivanes,; 2 July 1957 – 1 April 2022) was a Soviet and Russian actress and businesswoman. She was one of the most popular actresses in 1980s. She was in the Soviet disaster movie Air Crew (1979) had the first erotic scene in a mainstream domestic Soviet movie. Yakovleva died in Moscow, Russia on 1 April 2022 from breast cancer at the age of 64.

Aleksey Vladimirovich Batalov was a Soviet and Russian actor. He has been known for his portrayal of noble and positive characters. He was named a People's Artist of the USSR in 1976 and a Hero of Socialist Labour in 1989. He also starred in Mikhail Romm's Nine Days of One Year (1962). Alemayehu Eshete (; French pronunciation: Alèmayèhu Eshèté; June 1941 – 2 September 2021) was an Ethiopian jazz singer. His career began in the 1960s. Most of his music was in Amharic. He was nicknamed "the Ethiopian Elvis". Eshete was born in Jimma, Ethiopia. Eshete was popular in Europe with the release of Buda Musique's Ethiopiques series of compilations on compact disc. Eshete died on 2 September 2021 in a hospital in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia from a heart attack caused by heart disease at the age of 80.

Alene Bertha Duerk (March 29, 1920 – July 21, 2018) was a United States Navy admiral. She was born in Defiance, Ohio. She became the first female admiral in the U.S. Navy in 1972. She was also the director of the U.S. Navy Nurse Corps from 1970 to 1975. She was a 1974 recipient of a Distinguished Alumni Award of Case Western Reserve University's Frances Payne Bolton School of Nursing. Duerk died in Lake Mary, Florida on July 21, 2018 at the age of 98.
Alessandra Karpoff (Milan,1963) is an Italian voice actress. She is better known for her roles in Italian dubs of various anime as Misty from Pokémon.

Alessandra Sardoni (born 5 May 1964 in Rome) is an Italian journalist and television presenter. From 2013 to 2014, she was president of the Parliamentary Press Association. In June 2015, she was awarded the Premiolino. She studied with Tullio De Mauro. She worked for La Repubblica. She hosted the Otto e mezzo program and the Omnibus morning program.

Alessandra Watle Mele (born 5 September 2002), known mononymously as Alessandra, is an Italian-Norwegian singer. Alessandra Carina Mastronardi (born February 18, 1986) is an Italian actress. She is best known for her roles in the movies To Rome with Love and The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent. She also played Francesca in the television series Master of None.

Alessandro Scarlatti (born Palermo, 2 May 1660; died 24 October 1725) was an Italian composer. He lived in the Baroque period. He is especially famous for his operas and chamber cantatas. He is thought of as the founder of the Neapolitan school of opera. He was the father of the famous composer Domenico Scarlatti. Scarlatti was born in Palermo. At that time it was part of the Kingdom of Sicily. We know nothing about his musical education. When his opera Gli Equivoci nell sembiante was produced in Rome in 1679 the Queen of Sweden, who was living in Rome at the time, was very impressed and gave him the job of being her Maestro di cappella. In February 1684 he became Maestro di Cappella to the viceroy of Naples. He wrote many operas for him, as well as some music for important state occasions. In 1702 Scarlatti left Naples and went to Florence where he composed operas for Ferdinando de' Medici and for Cardinal Ottoboni, who made him his maestro di cappella. In 1703 he also got a similar job in Rome at the Basilica di Santa Maria Maggiore. After visiting Venice and Urbino in 1707, Scarlatti went back to Naples in 1708, and stayed there until 1717. However, the audiences in Naples no longer seemed interested in his music. They liked their serious operas to include comic music. Some of his best operas were written for Rome where they were produced at the Teatro Capranica. He also wrote some church music and music for royal weddings. He died in Naples. Scarlatti's music forms an important link between the early Baroque Italian vocal styles of the 17th century and the classical period of the 18th century, which led to the music of Haydn and Mozart. Perhaps his greatest work is Mitridate Eupatore. Many of his later operas are full of music which allows the singers to show off. In his opera Teodora (1697) he was the first composer to use the orchestral ritornello (a tune which keeps coming back after sections of solo singing). Some of his later operas written for Rome make the orchestra sound much more modern. He uses horns in the orchestra. This was a new idea. As well as operas, Scarlatti composed at least five hundred chamber-cantatas. These are works for solo voice accompanied by the orchestra. Hardly any of them were published, but they contain a lot of good music. He also wrote masses including the St Cecilia Mass (1721).

Alessandro Striggio (about 1536–1592) was an Italian composer and Musician of the Renaissance period. His music was well known throughout Europe and he was very influential in England. His son, also named Alessandro Striggio, wrote the libretto for Monteverdi's Orfeo.

Alessandro Moreschi (11 November 1858 – 21 April 1922) was a castrato singer of the late 19th century and the only castrato to make solo recordings. All of Moreschi's recordings were made in Rome in two recording sessions for the Gramophone & Typewriter Company. The first series of recordings were made on 3 and 5 April 1902 by Will and Fred Gaisberg. Eighteen usable sides by the members of the Sistine Chapel Choir were made on wax. Four of them were solos by Moreschi. Many years later Fred Gaisburg remembered making these historic first recordings in the Vatican: "Selecting a great salon with walls covered with Titians, Raphaels, and Tintorettos, we mounted our grimy machine right in the middle of the floor." The second set of recordings was made in Rome in April 1904. Alessandro was a member of the Sistine choir until Easter 1913. He then retired and got a pension after thirty years' service. In retirement, Moreschi lived in his apartment, a few minutes' walk from the Vatican. He died there at sixty-three, possibly of pneumonia. His funeral mass was a large and public affair in the church of San Lorenzo in Damaso.

Alessia Caracciolo (born July 11, 1996), known professionally as Alessia Cara, is a Canadian singer and songwriter. She is best known for her hit songs "Here" and "Wild Things". Cara's singing style has been compared to that of Norah Jones and Adina Howard. Cara released her first single "Here" in April 2015. The following single, "Scars to Your Beautiful", was released from her first studio album, Know-It-All. She collaborated with German DJ Zedd on the song "Stay". "Stay", "Here", and "Scars to Your Beautiful" all reached the top ten in the US and was at the top of the US Mainstream Top 40 radio chart. In 2018, she won the Grammy Award for Best New Artist, one of the "Big Four" awards.

Alexandrea "Alex" Borstein (born February 15, 1971) is an American actress, voice actress, writer, and comedian. Borstein is known for her long running role as Lois Griffin in the animated television series Family Guy, and a cast member on the sketch comedy series MADtv. Born in Highland Park, Illinois and studied San Francisco State University. Borstein was trained in comedy at the ACME Comedy Theatre, near Hollywood, California, and was selected to join MADtv after being searched by talent agents who noticed her comedy work at the theatre. Borstein was a writer and voice actress for several shows like; Casper, Pinky and the Brain and Power Rangers: Zeo, Powerpuff Girls, before joining the cast of MADtv as a featured player, and as a theatre player in 1997.
